facts.text: Originally called El Presidio and designed in the Streamline Moderne style.
Reopened on Christmas Day 2004 as a four-screen cinema after a remodel by Lee Neighborhood Theaters.

name: Presidio Theatre
note: Source dates the original building to 1939; OSM says 1938.

facts.text: Built by the U.S. Army with WPA funding, as a theater for soldiers and their families.
Reopened as a performing arts center after a $44 million renovation that began in 2017.
Opened in 1978.
Has Legacy Business status from the City of San Francisco.
Has a sister club in Sacramento.
Has RPX with HDR by Barco and a ScreenX auditorium.

name: Roxie
note: Little Roxie is at 3125 16th St; main Roxie is at 3117 16th St.

facts.text: Became a stand-alone nonprofit 501(c)(3) in 2009.
Taken over in March 1976 and turned into an art and independent film house.
A second screen, the Little Roxie, opened in 2003.

name: San Francisco Playhouse
note: No address given; matched to current home at 450 Post Street, about 100 m away.

facts.text: A nonprofit theater company founded in 2003 by Bill English and Susi Damilano.
Received the American Theatre Wing's National Theatre Company Grant in 2015.
Runs a Rising Star Program that provides theater tickets to under-served youth.
Covers about 100 acres in the southwest corner of the city, next to Lake Merced and the Great Highway.
Owned by the city Recreation and Park Department and managed by the nonprofit San Francisco Zoological Society.
Birthplace of Koko the gorilla.
Founded in 1993 by Matt Shelton and part of the Shelton Studios arts community, founded in 1961.
Hosts stand-up comedy, improv and art shows in two venues of 102 and 70 seats.
Also offers acting and improvisation classes.
Moved to Fisherman's Wharf from its earlier site in Golden Gate Park.
Hosts free daily street performer shows, weather permitting, at the bay end of Pier 39.
Has an elevated proscenium stage and seats 162.
Located in Building D of Fort Mason Center.
Paid for by Claus Spreckels after his son Adolph, Park Commission president, persuaded him to fund a larger bandshell.
Its two relief sculptures are by Robert Ingersoll Aitken.
Damaged in the 1906 and 1989 earthquakes and renovated several times.
A.C.T. bought the historic cinema in February 2012 and reopened it as a theater in spring 2015.
Has a 283-seat theater and a 120-seat event and performance space, the Rueff Cabaret Space.

name: The Alcove Theater
note: Yelp title marks 414 Mason St as CLOSED (updated May 2026); snippet says New Musical Theater of San Francisco is focusing on site-specific work.

facts.text: A flying-theater ride at the entrance to Pier 39 that takes riders over San Francisco landmarks.
Moved here from the Mission after the founders found a basement space on a 15-year lease.
Began presenting shows in this North Beach space in August 2022.

name: The Lost Church
note: Page title: '65 Capp is now Bane Gallery'; the venue moved to 988 Columbus Ave in North Beach.

name: The Magic Theatre
note: No address given; Fort Mason Center, same building as Southside Theater.

facts.text: Founded in 1967 and one of Fort Mason's first resident nonprofit companies, from 1976.
Staged the world premieres of Sam Shepard's Buried Child in 1978 and True West in 1980.

name: The Marrakech Magic Theater
note: Confirmed open at 419 O'Farrell St via Yelp listing updated September 2026; no single-page facts available.

facts.text: Began in 1989 as a Monday night performance series at the Hotel Utah.
Moved to this Valencia Street building in December 1992 and bought the whole building in 1996.
Also has a second venue in Berkeley.
Designed by architect Albert Roller and opened in 1958 as the Grand Masonic Auditorium.
Hosts the annual meeting of the Masons of California and is a concert venue the rest of the year.
Its facade carries a frieze by Emile Norman.
A 40,000-square-foot nightclub and performance venue with a warehouse and an outdoor stage.
A children's theater offering pretend-play theater classes, camps and productions.
The renovated theater was inaugurated in March 2018.
Also called the Theatre Erick Moreau.
Built in 1910 as the Columbia Theater and long known as the Geary Theater.
Renamed for Toni Rembe after a $35 million anonymous gift, the largest in A.C.T. history.
